glosses: To grip suddenly; to seize; to clutch.

examples.text: I grabbed her hand to pull her back from the cliff edge.

Old Applegate, in the stern, just set and looked at me, and Lord James, amidship, waved both arms and kept hollering for help. I took a couple of everlasting big strokes and managed to grab hold of the skiff's rail, close to the stern.

glosses: To make a sudden grasping or clutching motion (at something).

examples.text: The suspect suddenly broke free and grabbed at the policeman's gun.
Stop grabbing or I won't give you any cookies.

glosses: To restrain someone; to arrest.
To grip the attention of; to enthrall or interest.

examples.text: How does that idea grab you?

Baby, instant soup doesn't really grab me
Today I need something more substantial

glosses: To quickly collect, retrieve, or take.

examples.text: Come in and grab a seat [i.e. sit down].
"I'll just grab my jacket," said Manh-Hung.
Hardly believing that Rafe actually planned to relax for a while, Kate nodded. "All right. Fine. I'll just go grab my purse."
He looked at Albert and Ben, and then back to Nurse Allen. "I'll just grab my gear and be right back."

glosses: To consume something quickly.

examples.text: We'll just grab a sandwich and then we'll be on our way.
Is there time to grab a coffee?

glosses: To take the opportunity of.

examples.text: Both teams wasted good opportunities to score but it was the London side who did grab what proved to be the decisive third when the unmarked Vaz Te, a January signing from Barnsley, drilled the ball into the net from 12 yards.

glosses: A sudden snatch at something.

examples.text: The ball popped in and popped out, and when he made a grab for it on the ground he kicked it with his foot.
He made a grab for me and I swung my handbag at him as hard as I could.

glosses: An acquisition by violent or unjust means.
A mechanical device that grabs or clutches.

examples.text: Almost all modern cranes are electrically operated and a quick-acting type of 30 cwt. capacity is suitable for general cargo, but not powerful enough to operate grabs for discharge of bulk cargoes.

glosses: A mechanical device that grabs or clutches.
A device for withdrawing drills, etc., from artesian and other wells that are drilled, bored, or driven.
A sound bite.

examples.text: For example, one radio bulletin may feature one central issue, like a state election, and will focus on that issue. The bulletin might contain only a few voice wraps but many grabs, leaving the focus firmly on the newsreader.

glosses: That which is seized.
The rescue of a person from a burning structure.

examples.text:
2022, Mark van der Feyst, Matt Wehrle, Rob Wiggins, The Tactical Firefighter
There have been many rescues made as a result of an aggressive search team who went in without a hoseline to make the grab.

glosses: A simple card game.
A two- or three-masted vessel used on the Malabar coast.
To get to work; to focus on a task.

examples.text: You should knuckle down and do your homework!

As students all over the United States knuckle down to learning, the rumble of war drums once more proclaims Mars high man in Europe. Discarding morbid curiosity, every student should consider it vitally necessary to get a general picture of the causes, movements, and possible effects of World War II. The average U. S. citizen's knowledge of World War II will probably decide his role in it.

glosses: To submit; knuckle under.
To bring or come down; to descend; to cause to bring or come down.

examples.text: The kitten climbed the tree, but then couldn't get down again.
Don't worry, I got the kitten down.

glosses: To swallow (something).

examples.text: The pill was so large that he couldn't get it down.

glosses: To duck or take cover, usually to avoid harm. Commonly used as a caution or warning in the imperative.

examples.text: With bullets flying, all I could do was get down and pray.

glosses: To concentrate; attend.

examples.text: To get down to the matter at hand.

glosses: To depress; discourage; fatigue.

examples.text: Nothing gets me down so much as a rainy day.

glosses: To relax and enjoy oneself completely; be uninhibited in one's enjoyment.

examples.text: Getting down with a bunch of old friends.
It's Friday, Friday / Gotta get down on Friday / Everybody's lookin' forward to the weekend, weekend

glosses: To dance, particularly without inhibition or restraint, or in a sexually suggestive manner.
To party.
To have sex.

examples.text: She's always willing to get down with him.
And women will not care if Dick finally got down with Jane on Search for Tomorrow
Oh, do a little dance / Make a little love / Get down tonight, get down tonight
You get naked, honey, I'll get down / I'm gonna chase you around

glosses: To leave the table after dining.

examples.text: Mummy, can I get down please?

glosses: To record, most often in writing.

examples.text: Quick, here's a pen, get this down will you, before I forget.
They got the whole song down in an hour.

glosses: To criticise; to be strict towards.

examples.text: Ann is always getting down on these students.

glosses: To use a drug, especially heroin.

examples.text: I can't wait to get home and get down.

glosses: To do or perform well; to make happen; to make a serious effort at doing something.

examples.text: I've got this process down.

glosses: To bet on (something); to place bets; to gamble.

examples.text: He's gotta get down on this sure thing.

glosses: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see get, down.
To bind (a baby) with long narrow strips of cloth.
To beat; cudgel.
Anything used to swaddle with, such as a cloth or band.

examples.text: They put me in bed in all my swaddles.
The baby is awake, trying to escape the swaddle I have imprisoned her in.
